name: Wrought iron: puddled bar, plate and angle
summary: Nearly pure iron with threads of glassy slag drawn through it, made by puddling pig iron and rolling the balls into bar, plate and angle: tough, fibrous, forgeable and forge-weldable. In Albion it makes everything that carries the glass above the shafts: the riveted box girders on the arcade lines, the built-up main ribs and the T ribs, purlins and glazing bars, the end screens' mullions and transoms, the lancets' saddle bars, and the forged rings in the arcade spandrels; always seen painted.

identity.class: ferrous; ferrite with 1-2 % entrained siliceous slag, hot worked (not melted), fibrous

chosenBecause.text: It is the iron of Victorian girders, roof ribs and smiths' ornament; at Oxford the decorative spandrels of branches (sycamore, walnut, palm and others) are wrought iron.

chosenBecause.text: Wrought iron is no longer made: the last works, the Atlas Forge of Thomas Walmsley and Sons in Bolton, closed in 1973 (Engine Shed says it 'hasn't been made since the 1960s'). The museum depicts it; Matter records the real thing.

formation.how: Puddling (Henry Cort, 1784): pig iron is melted in a reverberatory furnace, where the fuel never touches the metal, on a hearth lined with iron oxides. The puddler stirs the bath; the carbon burns out, the iron thickens into a pasty mass, and he gathers it into balls (charges of up to about 200 kg, balls of about 50 kg). The balls are hammered (shingled) to squeeze out most of the slag and rolled to 'muck bar'; bars are cut, piled and rolled again for better grades, which draws the remaining slag into long threads. The result is nearly carbon-free iron with a grain like wood: a fresh fracture is bluish, silky and fibrous, and rust or etching brings the grain up.

optics.note: Victorian iron is never seen bare in Albion: it is always under its paint (painted.iron), whose optics are a dielectric coat. For a cut or worn-through edge, the bare metal's constants are those of iron, already recorded (Johnson and Christy 1974) in the steel record; a grey cast iron's graphite flakes and a wrought iron's slag stringers lower and darken a bare face but were not measured here.

spectral.text: Iron n,k (0.381-0.756 um) and the derived F0 and F82 triples are in the steel record; they are not copied here.

acoustic.note: Slender members overhead under the glass; not an absorbing surface. The rain drumming on the ribs is Sound's (see cast-iron).

forms.text: Rolled bar (flat, round, square), plate and angle, joined by hot rivets into girders and ribs, or forged by the smith; 'hand-worked through heating, hammering, and rolling'.

asBuilt.text: Painted as the cast iron (MI_Albion_Iron); the paint's values are in painted.iron.

photograph: Painted like the cast iron, but the members are thin and built up: plates and angles with rows of domed rivet heads along every seam, the ribs' flanges reading as crisp lines against the glass.
Forged work (the spandrel rings) has hammer-soft arrises, tapering scrolls, collars and forge-welded joints, never the parting lines of a casting.
Where it has rusted under failed paint, wrought iron swells and splits along its grain into layers, and thin members bend.

familyDeclaration.text: D-014 admits the families stone, white, bronze, oak, accent, glass, water and living; an accent names the core family it ties back to. Albion's iron exists to carry the glass of the vaults and screens (the stone stops at the capitals; above 6.2 m everything is iron and glass), as the Rotunda's steel lattice does, so it is declared an accent of the glass family, the same reading the metal group made for steel. The Architect may overturn it.
